translations.text: When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, and so on.
"At one time the Saviour was travelling to Jerusalem. When he drew near the city and saw it, he wept over it," and so on.

Gregory the commentator said that the Saviour wept for the destruction of the city, which happened after his passion as punishment for their wicked deeds, because they wickedly meant to kill the heavenly Prince.
He spoke with a weeping voice, not to the building stones or to the structure, but to the citizens, whom he mourned with a father's love, because he knew their ruin was soon to come.
For a period of forty years God's mercy allowed the cruel citizens time to repent of their wicked deeds, but they paid no heed to any penance,
but committed greater crimes, so that they stoned Stephen, God's first martyr, and beheaded James, the brother of John.
They also pushed the righteous James off the temple and killed him, and they persecuted the other apostles.
God's church, which after Christ's passion had been living in that city under James the Righteous, left the city all together for a town by the river Jordan;
because God's command came to them that they should leave that wicked place before the vengeance came.
Then God saw that the Jews paid no heed to any penance but kept adding more and more to their crimes. So he sent the Roman people against them, and they destroyed them all.
The emperor who ruled the kingdom of the whole world in those days was called Vespasian. He sent his son Titus to conquer the wretched Jews.
It so happened that six hundred thousand people were gathered inside the city of Jerusalem, shut in as if in a single prison;

and then they were besieged from outside by the Roman army for so long that many thousands there died of hunger. Because there were so many, they could not be buried, so the bodies were thrown over the wall.
Some, however, wanted to bury them out of love for their kin, but they soon died of weakness.
If anyone prepared a little food of any kind for himself, robbers rushed at him at once and snatched the food from his mouth.
Some chewed their shoes, some their clothes, some straw, because of the great torment of burning hunger.
It is not fitting for us to recount in this holy gospel all the shameful miseries that happened to the besieged Jews before they would surrender.
Then most of the impious people were killed by that shameful famine, and the Roman army slew those the famine had left,
and they razed the city to the ground, so that not one stone was left there on another, just as the Saviour had earlier foretold with weeping.
Of the boys who were under sixteen years old, they sent ninety thousand away to various nations as slaves, and nothing of that accursed race remained in the land.
Afterwards the city was rebuilt in another place and settled with Saracens.
The Saviour revealed the reason for this destruction of the city when he said, "Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation."
He visited the citizens through his incarnation, but they did not keep him in mind, neither out of love nor out of fear.
The prophet spoke about this negligence with a complaining voice, saying, "The stork and the swallow kept the time of their coming, and this people did not recognize God's judgement."
The Lord said to the city, "If you knew what is coming to you, you would weep with me. Truly, on this day you live in peace, but the coming punishments are now hidden from your eyes."
The citizens were living in worldly peace, as they carelessly gave themselves up to fleshly desires and gave little thought to the coming miseries, which were still hidden from them.
If she had foreseen that misery, she could not have enjoyed the prosperity of the present life with a carefree mind.
The Lord drove the merchants out of the temple, saying, "It is written that my house is a house of prayer, and you have made it a den of thieves."
The temple was consecrated to God, for his services and hymns of praise and for the prayers of the faithful; but the greedy high priests allowed trading to be carried on inside it.
When the Lord saw that wrong, he made a whip out of ropes and drove them all out with blows.
This driving-out signified the coming destruction by the Roman army, and that downfall happened most of all through the sins of the high priests who, [?]
…living within the temple, received the people's offerings with pretended holiness, and persecuted those who came to the temple without an offering.
What was the temple but a den of thieves, as it were, when the high priests were filled with such greed and allowed that deceitful trading inside the house of God?
It is written in another gospel that money-changers sat there, and that cattle, sheep and doves were sold there.
In those days, according to the ordinance of the old law, people offered cattle, sheep and doves as a sign of Christ's passion.
Then greed led the priests to have such livestock for sale there, so that if anyone came from far away and wanted to offer his sacrifice to God, he would have it ready to buy close at hand.
The Lord then drove such trading out of the holy temple, because it had not been built for any trade, but for prayer.
"Then the blind and the lame came to him, and he healed them, and he was teaching the people daily in the temple."
The merciful Lord, who lets his sun shine on the righteous and the unrighteous alike, and sends rain and the fruits of the earth to the good and the wicked, [?]
…would not withhold his teaching from the perverse Jews, because there were many good people among the wicked who were improved by that teaching, even though the perverse ones opposed it.
He also confirmed the teaching with miracles, so that the chosen would be all the more faithful,
and the reprobate would have no excuse, because they refused to believe in the true Saviour either through divine signs or through living teaching.
Now the blessed Gregory says that their destruction bears some likeness to every perverse person who delights in evil deeds and rejoices in the worst things.
The merciful Lord, who then mourned the doomed citizens with tears, grieves daily over such people.
But if they knew of the downfall that is coming upon them, they would mourn for themselves with a sorrowful voice.
Truly, this following saying applies to the soul that is perishing: "Today you live in peace, but the vengeance to come is now hidden from your eyes."
Truly, the perverse soul dwells in peace in its day, when it rejoices in this passing time, is lifted up with honours, is immoderate in transitory pleasures,
and is dissolved in fleshly lusts, and is not frightened by any fear of the punishment to come, but hides from itself the miseries that will follow;
for if it thought about them, its worldly joy would be troubled by that thought.
The soul has peace in its day when it refuses to weaken its present pleasure with any worry about future misfortune, and goes with its eyes shut to the fire of punishment.
The soul that now lives in this way is to be afflicted when the righteous rejoice;
and all the perishable things that it now counts as peace and joy will then be turned for it into bitterness and strife;
…because it is in great conflict with itself over why it would not, while still alive, take any care to foresee the downfall that it then suffers.
Of this it is written, "Blessed is the man who is always afraid; and truly the hard-hearted will fall into evil."
Again, in another place, holy scripture admonishes, "In all your works be mindful of your last day, and you will never sin."

The holy reading says, "The time will come when your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and hem you in on every side, and lay you low to the ground, together with your children who are within you."

The enemies of souls are the spirits of hell, who besiege a person's departure from this life and, if his soul is sinful, seek to lead it with great anguish into the fellowship of their own condemnation,
The devils show the sinful soul its evil thoughts, its harmful words and its wicked deeds, and torment it with many kinds of threats,
so that at its departure it may recognize by what enemies it is surrounded, and yet it finds no way out by which it might escape the hostile spirits.
It is laid low to the ground through the acknowledgment of its sins, when the body in which it lived has decayed to dust.
Its children fall in death when the unlawful thoughts it now conceives are utterly destroyed in the final vengeance,
as the psalmist sang about this: "Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the children of men, in whom there is no salvation.
Their spirit departs, and they return to the earth, and on that day all their thoughts perish."
Truly, it follows in the gospel: "And they will not leave in you one stone upon another."
When the perverse mind heaps evil upon evil and perversity upon perversity, what does it do but, as it were, lay stone upon stone?
But when the soul is led to its punishment, then the whole building of its scheming is thrown down, because it did not recognize the time of its visitation.
In many ways Almighty God visits the souls of men: sometimes with teaching, sometimes with miracles, sometimes with sicknesses;
…but if it ignores these visitations, then at its end it will be handed over for eternal punishment to the fiends whom it obeyed in life through grave sins.
Then those who earlier enticed it into sins with various desires will be its tormentors in the torment of hell.
The Lord went into the temple and drove out the traders with a whip. The traders within the temple signified unrighteous teachers in God's church.
Oxen, sheep, and doves were sold there, and money-changers sat there.

The ox tills for its lord, and the teacher sells oxen in God's church if he carries out his lord's tilling, that is, if he preaches the gospel to those under him for earthly gain and not for divine love.

He traffics in sheep if he seeks the praise of foolish men for his pious works. Of such the Saviour said, "They have received the reward of their works"; that is, the fame of empty praise that was pleasing to them.
The teacher is a seller of doves who will not use the gift that God gave him without his deserving it for the benefit of other men without payment;
as Christ himself taught: "Without price you received the gift; give it to others without price."
He who with feigned holiness labours for himself in God's church and cares nothing for Christ's tilling is without doubt counted a money-changer.
But the Saviour drives such merchants out of his house when he condemns them and cuts them off from the fellowship of his chosen.
"My house is a house of prayer, and you have made it a den of thieves."
It happens very often that the perverse come to high rank in God's church, and then by their wickedness they spiritually slay those under them, whom they ought to bring to life with their prayers.
What are such men but thieves? The mind of every believing person is God's house, as the apostle said: "God's temple is holy, which you are."
But that mind is not a house of prayer but a den of thieves if it loses the innocence and simplicity of true holiness and with perverse thoughts plots harm to others.
"And he was teaching daily in the temple."
Christ then taught the people in his presence, and he now daily teaches the minds of believing people with divine teaching, by careful thought, so that they may shun evil and do good.
It is not complete for the believer to cease from evil unless he does good.
The blessed Gregory said, "My brothers, I would like to tell you a little story, which can greatly edify your minds, if you will listen to it with attention.
There was a nobly born man in the province of Valeria named Chrysaorius, who was as greatly filled with sins as he was enriched with earthly wealth.
He was puffed up with pride, and subject to his fleshly lusts, and inflamed with immoderate greed.
But when God purposed to put an end to his wickedness, he fell sick and was brought to the point of death.

Then at the very hour when he was to die, he looked up, and black spirits stood around him and pressed upon him with great menace, so that they might seize his soul at his departure and take it with them to the prisons of hell.
He then began to tremble and turn pale and to sweat beyond measure, and with a great outcry to beg for a respite, and his son Maximus, whom I afterwards saw as a monk,
cried out in a troubled voice and said, "My child Maximus, help me; take me into your faith. I never did you harm in anything."
Then his son Maximus came to him, distressed and weeping bitterly. The man was writhing like a worm; he could not bear the terrible sight of the accursed spirits.
He turned toward the wall, and there they appeared to him; he turned back again, and there he found them.
When he was in such great anguish and had given up hope for himself, he cried out in a loud voice and said, "Give me time until morning, at least give me time until morning!"
but with this outcry the black fiends drew the soul out of the body and led it away."
From this it is clear that the vision was shown to him to make other people better, not for his own sake.
Lo, what did it profit him that he saw the black spirits at his departure, when he could not have the respite that he desired?
But let us take care that our time is not lost to us through idleness, so that we only want to turn to good deeds when death is pressing us to depart.
You, Almighty Lord, have mercy on us sinners, and so order our departure that, with our sins atoned for, after this perilous life we may be joined in fellowship with your saints.
To you be praise and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
